title: Spacing and Interleaving of Study and Practice https://basicknowledge101.com/pdf/science_of_learning.pdf
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), November 17, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton covers Shana Carpenter's chapter-length review of the spacing effect and the interleaving effect as two distinct but related learning strategies. Spacing refers to distributing study over time rather than massing it; interleaving means mixing different types of material rather than blocking practice by category. Carpenter surveys evidence across vocabulary learning, maths problem solving, and art history, and directly addresses why both strategies face resistance in real classrooms: students work more slowly and make more errors under interleaved conditions, which makes the approach feel less effective even as final-test performance improves. Barton draws out that most instructional materials — foreign language textbooks, maths workbooks — are organised by topic in a way that actively works against spacing and interleaving, meaning teachers usually have to deliberately restructure or supplement materials to get the benefit.
points: Interleaving different problem types improves long-term retention of maths, despite feeling harder and producing more errors during practice.
Students often resist spacing and interleaving because both make learning feel harder in the moment — teachers need to explain the trade-off explicitly.
Cumulative exams and quizzes double as spaced re-exposure and as motivation for students to independently review older material.
Most textbooks are organised by topic in ways that actively work against spacing and interleaving, so teachers typically need to supplement materials themselves.
quotes: The spacing effect refers to the benefit of studying material in spaced intervals rather than back-to-back, while interleaving emphasizes the advantages of mixing different types of material during learning instead of practicing one type of material exhaustively before moving on.
Students' retention of mathematics knowledge can be enhanced by interleaving different types of problems rather than blocking them by type.
Teachers should be aware that students may be reluctant to use spacing and interleaving because they perceive these methods as making learning more difficult.
Teachers should explain to students that even though interleaving may make learning feel harder initially, it is more effective for long-term learning than blocking.
Students work more slowly, and make more errors, when working a set of practice problems that is interleaved rather than blocked

Teachers may need to modify or supplement educational materials to ensure that students have the opportunity to use spacing and interleaving because textbooks and other materials do not always encourage these approaches.
